notes: The usual high-pressure definition preserves the professional 140/90 and home 135/85 thresholds, their inclusive boundaries and their separate settings.
The clinic measurement instructions preserve 3 to 5 minutes of rest, silence, unfolded legs, supported back and the arm at heart height.
The measurement instruction retains at least three readings at one-minute intervals and recording the average of the final two.
The significant inter-arm difference is retained as the trigger for using the arm with the higher readings.
Monitor compatibility, individual cuff sizing and the bladder length and width proportions of 75 to 100% and 35 to 50% of arm circumference all match.
The resistant-hypertension population and cardiovascular-event warning are now present alongside the cuff-over-clothing overestimation and false-diagnosis risk.
Home monitoring retains seven consecutive days, morning and evening sessions, appropriate training, three readings one minute apart and the mean of the second two.

Both symptom and autonomic-neuropathy-risk groups retain supine and standing measurements after at least one minute and consideration of postural hypotension at the 20 mmHg systolic and/or 10 mmHg diastolic falls.
The three hypertension patterns and differing haemodynamics remain distinct, with the young-adult isolated-systolic pattern, male and BMI associations and stroke-volume-driven output preserved.
The meta-analysis remains scoped to people on antihypertensive treatment and preserves a 3 grams/day salt reduction with an approximately 3.5/2 mmHg pressure fall.
The 6 to 8% body-weight reduction and associated 5/4 mmHg systolic/diastolic fall match, including the difficulty maintaining the change long term.
The lifestyle list keeps the regular 14-unit alcohol threshold, avoiding salty food or added salt, all three caffeine examples and not smoking.
The BIHS definition preserves clinic 140/90 and daytime ambulatory or home 135/85 thresholds, at least three optimal or tolerated drugs, ideal drug classes and both exclusions.
Both reported prevalence ranges, treated-adult population and the distinction between general reports and the BIHS definition match.
Inaccurate devices, wrong cuff size, white-coat readings, incompressibility from brachial calcification and non-adherence remain distinct causes of pseudo-resistance.
Specialist referral remains something to consider only after confirmed resistant hypertension, exclusion of pseudo-resistance and drug plus non-drug measures leave pressure above target.
Adult specialist referrals retain the likely-management-change scope and both branches: emergency referral for life-threatening organ damage and routine referral with the three examples.
The emergency or same-day referral definition preserves malignant hypertension, hypertensive crisis, and both pregnancy-related entries.
The precondition for routine hypertension referral remains confirmation by either ambulatory or home monitoring, with neither monitoring branch lost.
Specialist review remains recommended for adults diagnosed below age 40, for both excluding secondary causes and optimising treatment.
The young-onset population, irreversible end-organ damage and need for prompt management to reduce lifetime cardiovascular risk are all retained.
The above-180/120 mmHg trigger, urgent assessment and instruction to follow BIHS hypertensive-crisis guidance are all present.
Severe hypertension without life-threatening end-organ damage retains reduction over days to weeks rather than hours and oral rather than intravenous therapy.
The emergency definition retains sustained pressure over the next few hours, progressive life-threatening damage and every listed emergency including both severe pre-eclampsia and eclampsia.
The typical diastolic threshold of at least 120 mmHg, bilateral grade 3 or 4 retinal findings, vascular mechanism and usual uncontrolled chronic-hypertension setting match.
Immediate attention, usually parallel assessment, the 6-to-24-hour partial reduction limits, both diastolic targets and the acute-aortic-syndrome exception match.
Upward-shifted autoregulation in chronic hypertension and impaired autoregulation in malignant hypertension retain the warning about organ perfusion at low pressures.
Labetalol remains commonly first line rather than mandatory, with its alpha/beta action, all three highlighted emergencies, vasodilators and parallel assessment preserved.
Oral rather than intravenous treatment is retained for uncomplicated malignant hypertension, together with both emergency and multi-organ-damage exceptions.
Eye-changes-only malignant hypertension retains gradual blood-pressure targets of below 200/120 within 24 hours, below 160/100 within a week and below 140/90 within 6 to 12 weeks as examples.
The uncertainty about drug choice, all three example regimens and doses, low phaeochromocytoma suspicion and prohibition of short-acting nifedipine are preserved.
Young-onset hypertension in women of childbearing potential remains the scope, with pregnancy and contraception discussions, conditional drug-harm advice and all three alternative drug examples.
The organ-strain statement and all six serious outcomes remain conditional on high pressure and, for increased disease risk, lack of treatment.
The worldwide leading modifiable cardiovascular risk-factor status and contributions to kidney disease, heart failure and dementia are preserved.
The trial report retains the 120 mmHg floor below age 75, 10% fewer events per 5 mmHg and both age-specific hazard ratios with their confidence intervals.
